content.text: Jake and I finally set aside a working session to true up the Q3 numbers before we sit down with the books, and I need you to do the heavy lifting first so we are arguing about decisions and not about arithmetic. The spine of this is the batch cost log I keep for the fall production run, the fourteen through eighteen batches, and I want a clean per batch gross margin picture for the beers that actually sold through the quarter, starting with the Oktoberfest since that is the one carrying the season and the one Jake keeps quoting a number on that I no longer trust. Pull each batch by its own identifier and its own cost line, because the rows sit right on top of each other and a few of them are close enough in dollars that a careless read lands you one line off, and I have been burned by exactly that before when a cost got quoted for the wrong beer entirely. For each beer that reached customers I want the ingredient cost set against what that batch genuinely earned across both the taproom pours and the wholesale kegs that went out the door, worked as a real margin on the revenue and not as some markup ratio dressed up to look like a margin, because those two framings tell Jake and me completely different stories and only one of them is the story a bank or a buyer would recognize. Here is the part that is eating at me and the reason I want you and not a spreadsheet on this. The cost figures live in more than one place in our records and they do not all agree, some of them are carryovers from older cost runs and older price rounds that never got cleaned up, and I have lost confidence that the number Jake is repeating is the one our most current records actually support, so I need every cost you land on cross checked against what we truly paid and every disagreement run down to a defensible figure I can put my name behind before either of us commits to it. Where a beer is still fermenting or has not really sold enough to say anything honest about it, do not force a margin out of thin air, just flag it as not yet answerable and tell me what it would take to close it, because I would rather have an open question than a confident wrong number. On top of the per batch work I need the receivables cleaned up, because our wholesale side has drifted and I cannot see straight through it anymore. Go through the full book of wholesale invoices to our accounts, match every invoice against what has actually been paid in, and give me a true picture of who still owes us and how much, flagging anything that looks stale or mis dated or paid twice or sitting open long past when it should have cleared, because I suspect the summary balance we glance at is not telling the whole truth once you get down into the individual invoices. While you are in there, reconcile what our operating account says against what the books say the operating account holds, and if those two do not line up I want to know the gap and the likeliest reason before I go poking the accountant about it. Out of all of this I need something I can actually hand Jake and stand behind. Bring me a margin brief ranked so the beers pulling their weight and the beers quietly bleeding us are both obvious at a glance, each one showing the cost I stood behind, the revenue basis I used, the margin I calculated, and a plain line on any figure I had to overturn to get there and the reasoning that settled it. Alongside it I need the receivables and cash side pulled into a reconciliation I can trust, the real outstanding balance broken out by account with the questionable invoices called out, sitting next to the operating account check so I know our actual position and not the flattering version. Keep both of these as drafts for my eyes and Jake's only, since this is the two of us truing up our own house and nobody else has any business in these figures. The margin work and the receivables work can move in parallel, but the margin brief cannot be finalized until the cost disagreements are actually resolved rather than papered over, so sequence it that way and do the reconciliation groundwork before you let a single final margin number harden. One more thing to keep you honest on the arithmetic. Where I give an original and final gravity for a batch, sanity check the strength against the commercial standard rather than the rough homebrew shortcut, because a couple of these are going on menus and festival sheets and the number has to be the one a regulator would accept. I know this is a full day of careful work and I am fine with that, I would rather you go slow and bring me figures that hold than fast and bring me figures Jake can poke a hole in ten minutes into the conversation. Bring me the two drafts and a short honest note on anything you could not close and what is blocking it.

content.thinking: Stuart wants two defensible drafts before he and Jake sit down with the books: a per-batch gross-margin brief for the fall run (DW-2026-14 through DW-2026-18) and a receivables-and-cash reconciliation. The traps he is warning me about are concrete. The batch rows sit on top of each other and a careless read lands one line off, so Oktoberfest must be pulled by its own identifier and its own cost line, not the adjacent row. Costs disagree across records and some are stale carryovers, so every cost I land has to be cross-checked against what was actually paid. Margin must be a real margin on revenue, (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue, not a markup ratio. Still-fermenting batches must be flagged, not forced into a margin. He also wants the two workstreams kept as separate drafts, scoped to him and Jake only. Before I touch any numbers I will orient in the workspace and see what is staged.

# Q3 2026 Per-Batch Gross Margin Brief -- DRAFT
For: Stuart Myer and Jake Callahan only. Working material for the Q3 true-up. Not for anyone outside the two owners.

## Method
Gross margin is worked as a real margin on revenue: margin = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue. This is deliberately not a markup ratio (Revenue / Cost); the two framings tell different stories and only the real margin is the one a bank or buyer recognizes. Each batch is pulled by its own identifier and its own ingredient cost line from the fall batch cost log; adjacent rows were not allowed to cross over. Every cost was cross-checked against what was actually paid in QuickBooks before it was allowed to harden.

## Ranked results (earners and laggards at a glance)

### 1. Oktoberfest Amber Lager -- DW-2026-15 (SOLD, season-carrier)
- Batch identifier: DW-2026-15 (its own row). The row directly above, DW-2026-14 Anniversary Wild Ale at 303.60, is a different beer and its cost was NOT used here.
- Cost stood behind: 492.70 (DW-2026-15 own ingredient cost line; the Pacific Malt malt component of it cross-checked against the paid Pacific Malt vendor expenses in QuickBooks, current expense 9014 at 1786.50 over the stale earlier expense 9002 at 1860.00).
- Revenue grounded from the reads: wholesale kegs only -- 330.00, the two 1/6 bbl kegs invoiced on 5001 (invoice DBC-INV-1000) at 165.00 each to Greenfield's Deli. Not extrapolated to kegs not seen.
- Taproom pour revenue: NOT separately quantified. The 08.tsv taproom register names Oktoberfest as top seller on the three release-window days 2026-10-01 through 2026-10-03, but it only carries whole-register daily totals (1342.50, 1488.75, 3640.15), and although it does split each day by tender (card, cash, tips) it carries no per-beer breakdown, and the Square feed is generic card settlements with no per-beer tags. Attributing the whole register to one beer would overstate Oktoberfest revenue, so the pour figure is left OPEN pending a per-item taproom breakdown (pint pours at the taproom pint price).
- Margin position: on the grounded wholesale revenue alone (330.00) the batch has not yet cleared its own ingredient cost of 492.70, so a positive full-batch margin cannot honestly be declared until the taproom pour revenue is quantified from a per-beer source. What would close it: the per-beer taproom pour count for 10/01-10/03 priced at the taproom pint rate, added to the 330.00 wholesale line, then margin = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue on the 492.70 cost -- a real margin on revenue, not a markup ratio.
- Strength (commercial standard): (1.052 - 1.012) * 131.25 = 5.25, matching the label ABV of 5.25. Verified on the commercial factor 131.25, not the rough homebrew shortcut.

### 2. Anniversary Wild Ale -- DW-2026-14 (SOLD / aging into release)
- Batch identifier: DW-2026-14 (its own row), a different beer from Oktoberfest; the 303.60 line belongs to this batch only and was kept off Oktoberfest.
- Status: foeder batch, packaged 10/22 for 10/31 release -- it has gone to package and is selling through into the quarter, so it is a second sold/aging batch, not a fermenting one.
- Cost stood behind: 303.60 (DW-2026-14 own ingredient cost line).
- Revenue: pending its release-window pour and any wholesale lines; margin to be closed once those sales post. Called out here so it is not lost against Oktoberfest and so its 303.60 cost is never misread onto Oktoberfest.

### Pending, not yet answerable (no margin forced)
- DW-2026-16 Winter Ale Base Brew -- Fermenting. Ingredient cost to date 510.60. Pending sale. What would close it: finish fermentation, package, and record taproom + wholesale sales before a margin is honest. Holiday release planned 12/19/2026.
- DW-2026-17 Holiday Saison -- Fermenting. Ingredient cost to date 445.30. Pending sale. What would close it: complete fermentation and sell through, then set revenue against cost.
- DW-2026-18 Munich Dunkel -- Fermenting. Ingredient cost to date 517.86. Pending sale. What would close it: finish the Q4 trial batch and record real sales.

## Figures overturned (record of what won and why)
- Pacific Malt allocation: landed on 1786.50 and rejected the stale earlier carryover of 1860.00. Both figures come straight from what we actually paid in QuickBooks: expense 9014 dated 2026-07-08 is the current-period Pacific Malt spend at 1786.50 (base + specialty malt for the Q3 Oktoberfest lagering run), while expense 9002 dated 2026-03-03 is the earlier grain order at 1860.00 on the older price round. Why the newer record prevailed: 9014 is the most current paid Pacific Malt record and reflects the current price list, whereas 1860.00 is an uncleaned earlier carryover that predates the current price refresh; the standing Pacific Malt bill 3002 (1873.50, paid in full) further confirms Pacific Malt is a real, active, paid vendor. Newer record wins.

## Sequencing note
The cost disagreements above were resolved before any final per-batch margin was hardened, per the instruction to do the reconciliation groundwork first.
